qs.q: Which statement about the HTML DOM is correct?

c.x: The server creates it before sending the page, as a list of text lines
The browser creates it when the page is loaded, as a tree of objects
The browser creates it only after JavaScript runs, as a tree of objects
The developer creates it manually, as a tree of CSS rules

qs.e: When a web page is loaded, the browser creates a Document Object Model of the page, constructed as a tree of objects (document, elements, attributes, and text). JavaScript can then access and change all the elements of the document.

qs.q: In the statement below, which part is a method and which is a property? ```js document.getElementById("demo").innerHTML = "Hello World!"; ```

c.x: `innerHTML` is a method and `getElementById` is a property
Both `getElementById` and `innerHTML` are methods
Both `getElementById` and `innerHTML` are properties
`getElementById` is a method and `innerHTML` is a property

qs.e: Methods are actions you can perform, while properties are values you can set or change. `getElementById("demo")` is an action that finds the element, and `innerHTML` is a value (the content) that is assigned.

qs.q: You need <u>all</u> the elements that share the same class name. Which DOM method should you call?

c.x: `document.getElementById()`
`document.getElementsByTagName()`
`document.getElementsByClassName()`
`document.createElement()`

qs.e: `getElementById` finds one element by its id, `getElementsByTagName` finds elements by tag name, and `getElementsByClassName` finds elements by class name. `createElement` creates an element instead of finding one.

qs.q: Which statement changes the text color of the element with id `p2` to blue?

c.x: `document.getElementById("p2").color = "blue";`
`document.getElementById("p2").style.color = "blue";`
`document.getElementById("p2").innerHTML.color = "blue";`
`document.getElementById("p2").style = "color";`

qs.e: To change the style of an HTML element, use `element.style.property = new style`. Here the element is found with `getElementById("p2")`, and the property is `style.color`.

qs.q: Which pair of methods is used, <u>in this order</u>, to create a new HTML element and then add it to the page?

c.x: `createElement()`, then `removeChild()`
`write()`, then `removeChild()`
`appendChild()`, then `createElement()`
`createElement()`, then `appendChild()`

qs.e: `document.createElement(element)` creates an HTML element, and `appendChild(element)` adds it. `removeChild` removes an element, and `write` writes text into the HTML output stream.

c.x: `Qualifies for driving` in both cases
`Does not qualify for driving` in both cases
`Does not qualify for driving` for 15, and `Qualifies for driving` for 18
`Qualifies for driving` for 15, and `Does not qualify for driving` for 18

e: `15 > 18` is false, so the `else` block runs: Does not qualify for driving.
`18 > 18` is also false (the operator is `>`, not `>=`), so the `else` block runs again.
<mark>Both cases write: Does not qualify for driving.</mark>

c.x: `Entering Passed Not so good Exiting`
`Entering Unknown grade Exiting`
`Entering Passed Exiting`
`Entering Pretty good Passed Exiting`

e: The first `document.write` prints `Entering`.
`grade` is `'C'`, so execution jumps to `case 'C'` and prints `Passed`.
The `break` statement exits the switch block, so `Not so good` and `Unknown grade` are skipped.
The last `document.write` prints `Exiting`.
<mark>Output: Entering Passed Exiting</mark>

c.x: Neither loop writes anything, because the condition is false from the start
Both loops write `10`, because the condition is checked after the first pass
The `while` loop writes `10` once, and the `do...while` loop writes nothing
The `while` loop writes nothing, and the `do...while` loop writes `10` once

qs.e: `while` checks the condition <u>before</u> each pass, so with `n = 10` its body never runs. `do...while` checks the condition at the <u>end</u>, so its body always runs at least once: it writes `10`, then `n` becomes 11 and the loop stops.

qs.q:
How many times does the body of this loop run?
```js
for (i = 2; i < 10; i += 3) { /* body */ }
```
e: Initialization: `i = 2`.
Pass 1: `2 < 10` is true, the body runs, then `i` becomes 5.
Pass 2: `5 < 10` is true, the body runs, then `i` becomes 8.
Pass 3: `8 < 10` is true, the body runs, then `i` becomes 11.
`11 < 10` is false, so the loop stops.
<mark>The body runs 3 times.</mark>

qs.q: What does a `for...in` loop iterate over?

c.x: The properties of an object
The numbers from 0 up to a given limit
The statements inside a code block
The values returned by a dialog box

qs.e: The `for...in` loop is used to loop through an object's properties, as in the lecture's example that lists the properties of the `navigator` object.

e: `x = 1`: it is not 5, so `x` becomes 2 and `2` is written.
Likewise `3`, `4`, and `5` are written as `x` becomes 3, 4, and 5.
Now `x == 5` is true, so `break` exits the loop immediately, <u>before</u> anything else is written.
<mark>Written: 2 3 4 5</mark>

c.x: `5` is skipped, and eight numbers are written
`5` is skipped, and nine numbers are written
`5` is skipped and the loop stops there, with three numbers written
`1` is skipped, and eight numbers are written

e: `x` is incremented first, so the body sees the values 2 up to 10.
When `x` becomes 5, `continue` skips the rest of the body, so `5` is not written, and the flow goes straight back to the check `x < 10`.
<mark>5 is skipped, and 8 numbers are written.</mark>

c.x: `16` times
`12` times
`20` times
`8` times

e: For `i = 0`: `j` runs 0 to 3 and writes 4 times (`j = 4` triggers `break`).
For `i = 1`: the same, 4 more writes.
For `i = 2`: at `j = 0`, `break innerloop` exits the inner loop, so nothing is written.
For `i = 3`: 4 writes again.
For `i = 4`: at `j = 0`, `break outerloop` quits the outer loop completely.
<mark>Total: 4 + 4 + 0 + 4 = 12 writes.</mark>

qs.q: Which statement redirects the visitor to another page using JavaScript on the client side?

c.x: `window.location = "https://www.example.com";`
`window.redirect = "https://www.example.com";`
`document.write("https://www.example.com");`
`navigator.location = "https://www.example.com";`

qs.e: Client-side page redirection is done by assigning the new address to `window.location`, as in the lecture's `Redirect()` function.

qs.q: A page contains `setTimeout('Redirect()', 10000);`. Which statement is correct?

c.x: `Redirect()` is called every 10000 seconds
`Redirect()` is called 10000 times, once every second
`Redirect()` is called once after 10000 milliseconds, which is 10 seconds
`Redirect()` is called once after 10000 seconds

qs.e: `setTimeout(function, duration)` calls the function after `duration` milliseconds. 10000 ms equals 10 seconds, which matches the page message "You will be redirected to main page in 10 sec."

qs.q: Which option correctly matches each JavaScript dialog box with its purpose?

c.x: `alert()` shows a warning message; `confirm()` asks for confirmation (true/false); `prompt()` gets input from the user
`alert()` gets input from the user; `confirm()` shows a warning message; `prompt()` asks for confirmation (true/false)
`alert()` asks for confirmation (true/false); `confirm()` gets input from the user; `prompt()` shows a warning message
`alert()` shows a warning message; `confirm()` gets input from the user; `prompt()` asks for confirmation (true/false)

qs.e: The three dialog boxes are used to raise an alert, to get confirmation on an input, or to get input from the user: `alert()`, `confirm()`, and `prompt()` respectively.

c.x: `retVal` is `true`, so `User wants to continue!` is written and `true` is returned
`retVal` is `false`, so `User wants to continue!` is written and `false` is returned
`retVal` is `null`, so nothing is written and the function returns nothing
`retVal` is `false`, so `User does not want to continue!` is written and `false` is returned

qs.e: `confirm()` returns `true` when the user accepts and `false` when the user cancels. With Cancel, `retVal == true` is false, so the `else` block writes `User does not want to continue!` and returns `false`.

c.x: It raises an error, because `x` is not declared
It creates a global variable `x` with the value `3.14`
It creates a local variable `x`, because strict mode is declared at the top
It runs normally, because strict mode applies only inside functions

qs.e: Declared at the beginning of a script, `"use strict";` has global scope, so all the code runs in strict mode. Using a variable without declaring it is not allowed in strict mode, so `x = 3.14` causes an error.

qs.q: Which of the following is <u>not allowed</u> in strict mode?

c.x: Using a variable that was declared with `var`
Writing a method inside a class
Passing two different parameter names to a function
Deleting a function

qs.e: Strict mode does not allow undeclared variables or objects, deleting a variable, object, or function, duplicating a parameter name, octal numbers and escapes, and writing to read-only or get-only properties. The other options are ordinary, allowed code.

qs.q: Why do older versions of JavaScript simply ignore the `"use strict"` directive instead of failing?

c.x: Because it is a literal expression, not a statement
Because it is a keyword that older versions already know
Because it is written as a comment on its own line
Because it only works inside the `<head>` of the page

qs.e: `"use strict"` is not a statement but a literal expression, so versions of JavaScript before ECMAScript 5 ignore it.

qs.q: Which statement about a JavaScript class is correct?

c.x: It is an object itself, and it should always include a `constructor()` method
It is a template for objects, and it must not include methods other than `constructor()`
It is a template for objects, and it should always include a `constructor()` method
It is a template for objects, and it is created with the `function` keyword

qs.e: A class is created with the `class` keyword. It is <u>not</u> an object but a template for JavaScript objects. Always add a `constructor()` method, then any number of other methods.

e: `new Car("Audi", 2019)` stores `2019` in `this.year`.
`new Date().getFullYear()` returns the current year, `2030`.
<mark>11</mark>

c.x: `I have a Mustang, it is a Ford`
`I have a undefined, it is a Mustang`
`I have a Ford, it is a Mustang`
`it is a Mustang`

e: `new Model("Ford", "Mustang")` runs the `Model` constructor.
`super(brand)` calls the parent (`Car`) constructor, so `this.carname` becomes `"Ford"`; then `this.model` becomes `"Mustang"`.
`show()` calls `this.present()`, which `Model` inherits from `Car`, and it returns `"I have a Ford"`.
`show()` then appends `", it is a Mustang"`.
<mark>I have a Ford, it is a Mustang</mark>

qs.q: What is the role of `super(brand)` inside the constructor of a class that uses `extends`?

c.x: It creates a copy of the child class, to be used later as a new template
It declares the parent class and tells the browser to hoist it to the top
It removes the parent class so that only the child class remains in memory
It calls the parent's constructor and gives access to the parent's members

qs.e: The `super()` method refers to the parent class. Calling it in the constructor calls the parent's constructor and gives the child class access to the parent's properties and methods.

qs.q: A script creates an object with `new Car("Ford")` on its first line, and the `class Car { ... }` declaration appears <u>later</u> in the script. What happens?

c.x: It works, because class declarations are hoisted like functions
It works, but the object is created without calling the constructor
It raises an error, because class declarations are not hoisted
It raises an error only if the class has a method named `constructor()`

qs.e: Unlike functions and other JavaScript declarations, class declarations are <u>not hoisted</u>, so a class must be declared before it is used.

qs.q: Which option correctly describes the timer functions used in animations?

c.x: `setTimeout(f, d)` calls `f` once after `d` ms; `setInterval(f, d)` calls `f` every `d` ms
`setTimeout(f, d)` calls `f` every `d` ms; `setInterval(f, d)` calls `f` once after `d` ms
`setTimeout(f, d)` calls `f` once after `d` ms; `setInterval(f, d)` clears a timer set by `setTimeout()`
`setTimeout(f, d)` clears the timer; `setInterval(f, d)` calls `f` once after `d` ms

qs.e: `setTimeout(function, duration)` calls the function after `duration` milliseconds from now, `setInterval(function, duration)` calls it after every `duration` milliseconds, and `clearTimeout()` clears a timer set by `setTimeout()`.

c.x: Both `x` and `y` can be used outside the block
Neither `x` nor `y` can be used outside the block
`x` can be used outside the block, but `y` cannot
`y` can be used outside the block, but `x` cannot

qs.e: `let` and `const` provide block scope, so `x` cannot be accessed from outside the `{ }` block. Variables declared with `var` do not have block scope, so `y` can still be used outside the block.

c.x: Yes, because assigning to an undeclared variable makes it a global variable
No, because every variable assigned inside a function is local to it
No, because `carName` was never declared with `var`, `let`, or `const`
Yes, but only inside other functions, never in the main script

qs.e: If you assign a value to a variable that has not been declared, it automatically becomes a global variable, even when the assignment happens inside a function. Global variables can be accessed from anywhere in the program (in strict mode, however, this assignment would cause an error).

qs.q: Which is the shortest valid arrow-function version of `hello = function(val) { return "Hello " + val; }`?

c.x: `hello = val => return "Hello " + val;`
`hello = val -> "Hello " + val;`
`hello = => "Hello " + val;`
`hello = val => "Hello " + val;`

qs.e: If the function has only one statement that returns a value, the brackets and the `return` keyword can be removed. With only one parameter, the parentheses can be skipped too. The arrow is `=>` (not `->`), and `return` cannot stay once the brackets are removed.

qs.q: Which standard JavaScript statement does the same job as `myText = $("#id02").text();`?

c.x: `myText = document.getElementById("#id02").textContent;`
`myText = document.getElementsByClassName("id02").textContent;`
`myText = document.getElementById("id02").textContent;`
`myText = document.getElementsByTagName("id02").textContent;`

qs.e: jQuery's `$("#id02")` selects the element with id `id02`, and `.text()` gets its inner text. In standard JavaScript, that is `getElementById("id02")` (the id is written without `#`) followed by `textContent`.
